scenes.heading: Covalent bonding and molecular shape
scenes.sub: How sharing electrons decides a molecule's shape
scenes.say: Water, carbon dioxide, plastics and medicines are all held together by covalent bonds. The way atoms share electrons decides a molecule's shape, and that shape decides how it behaves.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Two players both gripping the same footy
scenes.science: Two nuclei both attracted to a shared pair of electrons
scenes.breaks: electrons aren't a solid ball in one spot; they're spread out as a cloud of negative charge.
scenes.say: Picture two players who both have their hands on the same footy and neither will let go. The footy is the shared pair of electrons, and the players are the two nuclei. Both are pulled towards the same ball, and that keeps them together. That's a covalent bond. A double bond is like gripping two footies at once.

scenes.heading: Covalent bonds
points: Non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons
Most atoms reach an octet (H needs 2)
HONC 1234: H 1, O 2, N 3, C 4 bonds
scenes.say: When two non-metals bond, they share electrons. A single bond is one shared pair, a double bond is two, and a triple bond is three. By sharing, most atoms reach a full outer shell of eight, or two for hydrogen. Remember HONC one two three four: hydrogen makes one bond, oxygen two, nitrogen three and carbon four.

scenes.heading: VSEPR: predicting the shape
steps: Count electron groups on central atom
Groups push as far apart as possible
Lone pairs push harder, squeeze angles
Name the shape from the atoms only
scenes.say: To predict a shape, use VSEPR theory: electron pairs around the central atom repel and move as far apart as they can. Count the electron groups. Lone pairs push a bit harder and squeeze the bond angles. Then name the shape from the positions of the atoms only, not the lone pairs.

scenes.heading: Four electron groups
scenes.say: With four electron groups and no lone pairs, like methane, the shape is tetrahedral at one hundred and nine point five degrees. One lone pair gives a pyramidal shape, like ammonia, at about one hundred and seven degrees. Two lone pairs give a bent shape, like water, at about one hundred and four point five degrees.
scenes.caption: With four electron groups and no lone pairs, like CH₄, the shape is tetrahedral at 109.5°. One lone pair gives pyramidal, like NH₃, at about 107°. Two lone pairs give bent, like H₂O, at about 104.5°.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: What is the shape of PCl₃, and is it polar?
lines: 3 P–Cl bonding pairs + 1 lone pair on P
P–Cl bonds are polar; shape is asymmetric
scenes.say: What shape is P C l three, and is it polar? Phosphorus has five valence electrons and each chlorine has seven, so twenty-six in total, or thirteen pairs. That gives three bonding pairs and one lone pair on phosphorus. Four groups with one lone pair means pyramidal. The bonds are polar and the shape isn't symmetrical, so the molecule is polar.
scenes.caption: What shape is PCl₃, and is it polar? P has 5 valence electrons and each Cl has 7: 26 in total, or 13 pairs. That gives 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair on P. Four groups, one lone pair: pyramidal. The bonds are polar and the shape isn't symmetrical, so it's polar.

scenes.heading: Is the molecule polar?
points: Polar bond: atoms differ in electronegativity
CO₂ is linear, so it's non-polar
Bent H₂O doesn't cancel, so it's polar
scenes.say: Polarity is a tug-of-war. A bond is polar when the two atoms have different electronegativities. But a molecule is only polar if those pulls don't cancel. Carbon dioxide is linear, so its two pulls point in opposite directions and cancel. Water is bent, so its pulls don't cancel, and water is polar.

points: Covalent bond = shared pair of electrons
Electron groups spread as far apart as possible
Name shapes from atoms, not lone pairs
scenes.say: Quick recap. A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons. Electron groups spread as far apart as they can, which sets the shape. Name the shape from the atoms, not the lone pairs. Polar bonds plus an uneven shape make a polar molecule. Now try the practice questions!
